summary: Perak stands under Malaysia's national framework. The source inventory assembled for this state contains no Perak-specific law, enforcement action, incident or institution: every documented item is national in scope or belongs to other Malaysian states, so the national assessment carried by the parent record applies here without state-level qualification.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement evidence assembled for this record is national or drawn from other Malaysian states, and none of it is attributable to Perak. The Human Dignity Trust country profile, last updated 16 December 2025, records no Perak-specific enforcement case among those it documents, and the Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters material released on 10 August 2022 names no Perak case either.

Because the inventory supplies no Perak figures alongside the national ones, it provides no basis for treating Perak as more exposed or less exposed than the country as a whole. Any ranking of Perak against other states on arrests, raids or violence would rest on data these sources do not contain.
localsOnly: No Perak-specific resident-facing finding appears in the inventory: no state institution, state penalty, state court decision, state religious-department operation or state government statement on LGBTQ enforcement is documented for Perak. Resident-facing exposure in the state is carried entirely by the national layer on the parent record, and by the state Sharia apparatus described there in general terms rather than through any Perak record.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Perak's own Sharia enactment sets penalties, procedures or institutional arrangements differing from the national pattern is unresolved here; the enactment's text and any Perak state amendments were not available in this inventory.

No Perak-specific record of arrests by the state religious department, of strip-search or detention practice, of violence against transgender residents, or of state government positions on LGBTQ enforcement was identified. These are absent from the sources rather than established as not having occurred.

The survey and interview material in the inventory is not disaggregated by state, so no Perak-specific count of affected residents, detainees or rehabilitation-programme participants can be derived from it.

Whether Perak courts have handled gender-marker, cross-dressing or section 377 matters, and how Perak's Registration Department office treats marker-change applications, are not sourced and remain open questions.
